body.statement: For every \(0<\alpha<1/2\), there are constants \(c_{\alpha},c>0\) such that every sequence of confidence intervals \(I_N\) with \(\liminf_N\inf_{(P_N,\mathcal S_N)\in\mathcal M}P_N\{\beta\in I_N\}\ge1-\alpha\) obeys \(\liminf_N\sqrt N\sup_{(P_N,\mathcal S_N)\in\mathcal M}E_{P_N}[\operatorname{length}(I_N)]\ge c_{\alpha}\), and every estimator \(\widetilde\beta_N\) obeys \(\liminf_N N\sup_{(P_N,\mathcal S_N)\in\mathcal M}E_{P_N}[(\widetilde\beta_N-\beta)^2]\ge c\).
body.justification: The converse certifies that the uniform profile procedure attains the honest length and risk rates even though \(p\) is unidentified at zero amplitude.
body.gap: Li's scalar microergodic Gaussian limit and Cai--Low's abstract modulus theory do not give a lower bound for the complete bivariate observed field with the slope and cross-tail nuisance.
body.consumer: It rules out claims that another spatial adjustment can uniformly deliver intervals of smaller order on the stated no-nugget model.
body.proof_tex:
Put \(\nu=(d+1)/2\).  We first exhibit a two-point subexperiment that remains inside \(\mathcal M\).  Fix the design sequence and a nuisance tuple \((c_X,c_W,\alpha_X,\alpha_W,\alpha_C)\in\mathcal K_{\mathrm{nuis}}\) supplied by the design and nuisance assumptions, fix any \(p^\circ\in[p_{\min},p_{\max}]\), and put \(A=0\).  The amplitude-space assumption permits this value.  Moreover, the determinant-margin assumption for any member of the model, together with \(f_Xf_W>0\), implies \(\rho\leq 1\).  Consequently the diagonal spectral matrix obtained when \(A=0\) satisfies
\[
 f_X(\omega)f_W(\omega)-0^2=f_X(\omega)f_W(\omega)
 \geq \rho f_X(\omega)f_W(\omega),\qquad \omega\in\mathbb R^d.
\]
Independent centered stationary Gaussian fields having the two marginal spectra therefore give an admissible \(A=0\) member of the Gaussian-field and spectral-family assumptions.  Keeping the prescribed sites and defining \(Y=\beta X+W\) verifies the observation-law assumption.  Thus every slope in \(\operatorname{int}(\mathcal B)\), with all these other quantities fixed, defines a submodel of \(\mathcal M\).

For the selected nuisance tuple define the finite constant
\[
 C_\star:=\frac{c_X}{c_W}
 \max\left\{1,\left(\frac{\alpha_W^2}{\alpha_X^2}\right)^\nu\right\}.
\]
Positivity of the nuisance coordinates, which is part of the nuisance-compactness assumption, gives \(0<C_\star<\infty\).  Directly from the two Mat\'ern marginal spectra,
\[
 \frac{f_X(\omega)}{f_W(\omega)}
 =\frac{c_X}{c_W}
 \left(\frac{\alpha_W^2+\|\omega\|^2}
 {\alpha_X^2+\|\omega\|^2}\right)^\nu
 \leq C_\star .
\]
Let \(\Sigma_{X,N}\) and \(\Sigma_{W,N}\) be the covariance matrices of
\(X_N=(X(s_{1,N}),\ldots,X(s_{N,N}))^{\mathsf T}\) and
\(W_N=(W(s_{1,N}),\ldots,W(s_{N,N}))^{\mathsf T}\), respectively.  For every \(z\in\mathbb R^N\), the spectral representation and the preceding pointwise inequality give
\[
 z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_{X,N}z
 =\kappa_d\int_{\mathbb R^d}f_X(\omega)
 \left|\sum_{i=1}^Nz_i e^{\mathrm i\omega^{\mathsf T}s_{i,N}}\right|^2d\omega
 \leq C_\star z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_{W,N}z,
\]
where the positive Fourier-normalization constant \(\kappa_d\) is the same for both spectra.  The integrals are finite because both spectra are bounded near zero and have radial tail of order \(\|\omega\|^{-(d+1)}\).  Separation makes the sites distinct.  If \(z\neq0\), choose a direction whose projections of the finitely many sites are distinct; linear independence of the resulting one-dimensional exponentials shows that the exponential sum in the display cannot vanish identically.  Since \(f_W>0\), the last quadratic form is then strictly positive.  Hence \(\Sigma_{W,N}\) is invertible and
\[
 \Sigma_{X,N}\preceq C_\star\Sigma_{W,N}.
\]
It follows that all eigenvalues \(\lambda_{1,N},\ldots,\lambda_{N,N}\) of
\(\Sigma_{X,N}^{1/2}\Sigma_{W,N}^{-1}\Sigma_{X,N}^{1/2}\) lie in \((0,C_\star]\), and
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_{i,N}
 =\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{W,N}^{-1}\Sigma_{X,N})
 \leq NC_\star. \tag{1}
\]

Choose \(\beta_0\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal B)\), as permitted by the slope-space assumption.  For a fixed \(q>0\), set
\(\Delta_N=qN^{-1/2}\) and \(\beta_{1,N}=\beta_0+\Delta_N\).  Since \(\beta_0\) is an interior point, \(\beta_{1,N}\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal B)\) for all sufficiently large \(N\).  At each such \(N\), denote by \(P_{0,N}\) and \(P_{1,N}\) the two \(A=0\) laws with slopes \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_{1,N}\).  Each law can be extended over all sample sizes with its slope held fixed, so both are \(N\)-th marginals of members of \(\mathcal M\).

Under \(P_{0,N}\), \(X_N\) and \(W_N=Y_N-\beta_0X_N\) are independent centered Gaussian vectors.  The conditional Gaussian density therefore gives the exact likelihood ratio
\[
 L_N:=\frac{dP_{1,N}}{dP_{0,N}}
 =\exp\left\{\Delta_NX_N^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_{W,N}^{-1}W_N
 -\frac{\Delta_N^2}{2}X_N^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_{W,N}^{-1}X_N\right\}. \tag{2}
\]
Taking the expectation of the log of the reciprocal likelihood ratio in (2), using independence and centering, yields the exact divergence
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(P_{0,N},P_{1,N})
 =\frac{\Delta_N^2}{2}
 \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{W,N}^{-1}\Sigma_{X,N})
 \leq \frac{q^2C_\star}{2}, \tag{3}
\]
where (1) proves the inequality.  We next derive, rather than assume, a total-variation bound adequate for both conclusions.  Conditioning (2) on \(X_N\) and using the moment-generating function of the centered Gaussian linear form in \(W_N\) gives
\[
 E_{0,N}[L_N^2\mid X_N]
 =\exp\{\Delta_N^2X_N^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_{W,N}^{-1}X_N\}.
\]
Diagonalizing the corresponding quadratic form in a standard Gaussian vector gives, whenever \(2\Delta_N^2C_\star<1\),
\[
 E_{0,N}L_N^2
 =\prod_{i=1}^N(1-2\Delta_N^2\lambda_{i,N})^{-1/2}.
\]
For all sufficiently large \(N\), \(2q^2C_\star/N\leq1/2\).  The elementary inequality \(-\log(1-x)\leq2x\) for \(0\leq x\leq1/2\), followed by (1), then implies
\[
 \log E_{0,N}L_N^2
 \leq \frac{2q^2}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_{i,N}
 \leq2q^2C_\star. \tag{4}
\]
By the definition of total variation and Cauchy--Schwarz,
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(P_{0,N},P_{1,N})
 =\frac12E_{0,N}|L_N-1|
 \leq\frac12\{E_{0,N}(L_N-1)^2\}^{1/2}
 \leq\frac12\{e^{2q^2C_\star}-1\}^{1/2}. \tag{5}
\]
Thus the full observed-field experiment cannot reliably distinguish slope changes smaller than a fixed multiple of \(N^{-1/2}\); no Fourier-coordinate independence has been used.

We first prove the interval assertion.  Put \(t_\alpha=1-2\alpha>0\) by the nominal-level assumption, and choose
\[
 q_\alpha=\left\{\frac{1}{2C_\star}
 \log\left(1+\frac{t_\alpha^2}{4}\right)\right\}^{1/2}>0.
\]
Equation (5) gives \(\operatorname{TV}(P_{0,N},P_{1,N})\leq t_\alpha/4\) eventually.  For a candidate interval sequence let
\[
 a_N:=\inf_{(P_N,\mathcal S_N)\in\mathcal M}P_N\{\beta\in I_N\}.
\]
Its assumed honesty says \(\liminf_Na_N\geq1-\alpha\).  Total variation and the union bound give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 P_{0,N}\{\beta_0,\beta_{1,N}\in I_N\}
 &\geq P_{0,N}\{\beta_0\in I_N\}
      +P_{0,N}\{\beta_{1,N}\in I_N\}-1\\
 &\geq 2a_N-1-\operatorname{TV}(P_{0,N},P_{1,N}).
 \end{aligned} \tag{6}
\]
On the event in (6), the interval has length at least \(\Delta_N\).  Therefore
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \liminf_N\sqrt N\sup_{(P_N,\mathcal S_N)\in\mathcal M}
 E_{P_N}[\operatorname{length}(I_N)]
 &\geq q_\alpha\liminf_N
 P_{0,N}\{\beta_0,\beta_{1,N}\in I_N\}\\
 &\geq \frac{3}{4}q_\alpha t_\alpha
 =:c_\alpha>0. \tag{7}
 \end{aligned}
\]

Finally, let \(\widetilde\beta_N\) be any estimator and choose
\[
 q_0=\left(\frac{\log2}{2C_\star}\right)^{1/2}.
\]
With \(q=q_0\), (5) gives \(\operatorname{TV}(P_{0,N},P_{1,N})\leq1/2\) eventually.  Define the test
\(\phi_N=\mathbf 1\{\widetilde\beta_N\geq(\beta_0+\beta_{1,N})/2\}\).  On \(\{\phi_N=1\}\) under \(P_{0,N}\), the squared error is at least \(\Delta_N^2/4\), and on \(\{\phi_N=0\}\) under \(P_{1,N}\), it is at least the same quantity.  Moreover, directly from the definition of total variation,
\[
 P_{0,N}\{\phi_N=1\}+P_{1,N}\{\phi_N=0\}
 \geq1-\operatorname{TV}(P_{0,N},P_{1,N}).
\]
Writing \(R_{k,N}=E_{k,N}[(\widetilde\beta_N-\beta_{k,N})^2]\), where \(\beta_{0,N}=\beta_0\), consequently yields
\[
 \max(R_{0,N},R_{1,N})
 \geq\frac{\Delta_N^2}{8}
 \{1-\operatorname{TV}(P_{0,N},P_{1,N})\}
 \geq\frac{q_0^2}{16N}.
\]
Both alternatives belong to \(\mathcal M\), so
\[
 \liminf_NN\sup_{(P_N,\mathcal S_N)\in\mathcal M}
 E_{P_N}[(\widetilde\beta_N-\beta)^2]
 \geq\frac{q_0^2}{16}
 =\frac{\log2}{32C_\star}=:c>0.
\]
Together with (7), this proves both claimed minimax lower bounds on the complete bivariate observed-field experiment.
